summary: Asks whether the Sharpe ratio is a sound measure of strategy quality. Argues conceptually (with citations) that it requires stationary, parametric returns, penalises upside, rewards tiny consistent returns and invites gaming. Recommends stationarity checks, semi-variance and long-term return under a risk constraint.

coverage.note: Sharpe definition, gaming, stationarity, parametricity, negative skew, footnote 1 Goetzmann
serial correlation, upside penalty, Sortino, tiny consistent profits, investor bias, recommendations, references

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: dividing the average period return in excess of the risk-free rate by the standard deviation of the return generating process
claims.claim: The Sharpe ratio is mean excess return over the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of returns; it has value as a quality measure but crucial limits.
claims.exact_rule: SR = mean(r_t - rf_t) / sd(r_t) over the evaluation period

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: its widespread and often indiscriminate adoption as a quality measure is leading to distortion of proper investment priorities, as investment firms manipulate strategies and data to maximise it.
claims.claim: Because investors reward high Sharpe ratios, managers engineer strategies and data to maximise the ratio rather than true quality.
claims.direction: be sceptical of very high reported Sharpe ratios
claims.testable: partly - compare Sharpe-maximising strategies with tail outcomes

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: whilst return is a definite and meaningful quantity (an “observable”), risk is not.
claims.claim: Return is observable but risk is not; standard deviation can always be computed but does not mean the same thing for every series.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: For the standard deviation to be a meaningful statistic at all the return time series must be generated from a process that is both stationary and parametric.
claims.claim: Standard deviation only measures risk if returns come from a stationary process with a parametric distribution.
claims.testable: partly - stationarity and distribution tests possible

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: A common violation of this in track records occurs when a manager’s style or leverage changes over the course of their history.
claims.claim: Stationarity (constant variance, skew, kurtosis) is often violated when a manager changes style or leverage over the track record.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: It is common for a manager’s early track record to differ significantly from later performance
claims.claim: Early track records often differ from later ones because a small manager can exploit a good anomaly or take big risks with little to lose.
claims.testable: yes - compare early vs late performance of managers

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: An increase in assets under management can enforce constraints on such opportunities, leading almost inevitably to a change in investment strategy.
claims.claim: Asset growth constrains capacity and almost inevitably changes the strategy, making the return process non-stationary.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: A simple test of rolling standard deviation through time (or even average period change) may be sufficient to uncover the manifestations of the resulting non-stationarity.
claims.claim: Rolling standard deviation and rolling mean return are a simple check for non-stationarity in a track record.
claims.exact_rule: Compute rolling sd (and rolling mean) of returns through the record; large shifts indicate non-stationarity (window not specified)

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: It is probably too demanding to ask that a manager’s record show no style drift at all
claims.claim: Some style drift is unavoidable in dynamic markets; aim for reasonable stationarity over the window used for statistics.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: In a non-parameterisable distribution, it conveys no information about anything.
claims.claim: Standard deviation conveys dispersion only for parametric distributions such as the normal; non-stationary distributions are non-parameterisable.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Cauchy-Paretian distributions have infinite variance
claims.claim: Fat-tailed (Cauchy-Paretian) return processes have infinite variance, so the Sharpe ratio cannot assess them.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: some will produce many small profits and the occasional large loss - before the loss has appeared such strategies will have a high Sharpe ratio!
claims.claim: Negative-skew strategies (many small gains, rare large loss) show high Sharpe ratios until the loss arrives.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Goetzman et al. explored the use of option-like strategies for engineering high Sharpe ratios without the need for manager skill (2002).
claims.claim: Goetzmann et al. (2002) showed option-like strategies can manufacture high Sharpe ratios without skill.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: sorts of distribution, vulnerable, like LTCM, to a major cataclysm.
claims.claim: Merger arbitrage and similar strategies have short-option-like return distributions exposed to rare cataclysms, as LTCM showed.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Some trading approaches which are swift to take profit but run losses may also twist the statistics to their advantage
claims.claim: Strategies that take profits quickly and let losses run can flatter their statistics.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: the serial correlation of monthly returns common in the more illiquid hedge fund strategies (e.g. convertible arbitrage) can lead to a substantial overstatement of Sharpe ratios
claims.claim: Serial correlation from illiquid pricing (e.g. convertible arbitrage) smooths monthly returns and substantially overstates Sharpe ratios (Asness et al. 2001; Lo 2001).
claims.exact_rule: Check autocorrelation of monthly returns; adjust Sharpe for serial correlation (Lo 2001)

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: large positive returns increase the perception of risk as though they could as easily be negative, which for a dynamic investment strategy may not be the case.
claims.claim: Standard deviation treats large gains as risk, which is wrong for dynamic strategies whose distribution is asymmetric.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: thus the removal of the highest returns from the distribution can increase the Sharpe ratio
claims.claim: Deleting the best returns can raise the Sharpe ratio, a reductio ad absurdum showing it penalises upside.
claims.testable: yes - easy to demonstrate on any positively skewed series

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: We might suggest an improvement by considering only the negative semi-standard deviation for the denominator, a measure known as the Sortino ratio.
claims.claim: Using downside semi-standard deviation (Sortino ratio) avoids penalising upside volatility.
claims.exact_rule: Sortino = mean excess return / downside semi-standard deviation (returns below target)

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: it still remains vital that the semi-standard deviation used is meaningful
claims.claim: The Sortino ratio still requires a stationary, well-understood distribution to be meaningful.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: a string of very small but consistent profits which will produce a very high Sharpe ratio with very little return.
claims.claim: Tiny but consistent excess returns (e.g. AAA commercial paper over government paper) give very high Sharpe ratios but show no skill.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Who would prefer to make 0.01% over risk-free each month rather than 1% with a standard deviation of 1%?
claims.claim: For such series raw return matters more: 1% a month with 1% sd beats 0.01% riskless excess, though Sharpe ranks it lower.
claims.reported_result: Example: 0.01%/month excess near-zero sd vs 1%/month with 1% sd

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: They are all mirrored in the (faulty) decision-making processes of investors who overvalue short run consistent returns and biased return-generating processes.
claims.claim: The distortions are real because investors overvalue short-run consistency, creating demand for Sharpe-gamed products.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: the danger of relying slavishly on any single measure for assessing product quality for risky investments.
claims.claim: No single statistic should be relied on to judge risky strategies.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: more use of semi- variance than variance as a risk measure; and a revival of return as a quality statistic (albeit long term return subject to some risk constraint).
claims.claim: Recommendations: check stationarity and parametricity, design flexible statistics, prefer semi-variance, and judge strategies on long-term return subject to a risk constraint.
claims.exact_rule: Evaluate strategies on long-run return subject to a risk limit; use semi-variance; test stationarity first
claims.indicator: long-term return under risk constraint; semi-variance

reasoning.question: Is the Sharpe ratio a valid universal measure of strategy quality, and what goes wrong when investors and managers optimise to it?

thesis.statement: The Sharpe ratio is only meaningful for stationary, parametric return processes and even then penalises upside and rewards tiny consistent returns; its indiscriminate use leads managers to game it, so investors should use several measures, semi-variance and long-term return under a risk constraint.

foundations.premise: Return is observable; risk is not directly observable.
Standard deviation measures risk only for stationary, parametric return processes.
Managers respond to what investors reward.

mechanism_chain.from: investors rank managers by Sharpe and overvalue short-run consistency

mechanism_chain.to: negative-skew, smoothed or option-like return streams
mechanism_chain.why: short-option payoffs, illiquid marking and take-profit/run-loss rules raise measured Sharpe

mechanism_chain.to: misleading Sharpe ratios and hidden tail risk
mechanism_chain.why: sd no longer describes the risk

design_rationale.choice: Use downside semi-deviation (Sortino) instead of sd
design_rationale.reason_given: does not penalise large positive returns

design_rationale.choice: Rolling sd / mean diagnostics before computing statistics
design_rationale.reason_given: reveal non-stationarity from style or leverage changes

design_rationale.choice: Long-term return subject to a risk constraint as a quality statistic
design_rationale.reason_given: Sharpe can favour tiny riskless returns over meaningful returns

evidence_map.result: Removing the highest returns can raise Sharpe
evidence_map.rules_out: Sharpe as a universal quality metric

evidence_map.result: Serial correlation overstates Sharpe in illiquid strategies (Asness et al.; Lo)
Option-like strategies engineer high Sharpe without skill (Goetzmann et al.)

regimes.condition: Before a tail event in negative-skew strategies
regimes.effect: Sharpe looks high; after the event it collapses
strategy changes and early record is unrepresentative

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: No empirical data, no thresholds for "reasonable stationarity", no rolling window length
Recommended "long-term return subject to some risk constraint" is not defined
Sortino has the same stationarity requirement, so the fix is partial by the author's own logic

relations.why: (reader) trend has upside volatility that Sharpe penalises, the opposite of take-profit/run-loss strategies
negative-skew strategies show high Sharpe until the crash

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Not a signal paper. For evaluating any macro backtest it implies: check rolling volatility/mean for stationarity, return autocorrelation (smoothing), skewness and tail losses, and upside vs downside deviation; a high Sharpe from a negatively skewed or smoothed series should be discounted. This stops mattering only if returns are close to i.i.d. normal.
reader_inferences: (reader) The critique implicitly favours positively skewed strategies such as trend following (Winton is a trend follower), which the Sharpe ratio understates.
(reader) Practical adoption rule for a macro book: report Sortino, skew, max drawdown and autocorrelation-adjusted Sharpe alongside Sharpe.
(reader) The 1%-mean/1%-sd example has a monthly Sharpe of 1, so it is the infinite-Sharpe riskless case that the Sharpe ratio would prefer.
